text.p: The following are the main stories from Thursday morning's German newspapers:
FRANKFURTER ALLGEMEINE ZEITUNG
- Chancellor Helmut Kohl's intelligence coordinator Bernd Schmidbauer defends actions of private detective Werner Mauss in bid to free German kidnap victim in Colombia.
- Science ministers from Kohl's Christian Democrats want to tie payments to universities more closely to their performance.
- Economic growth for third quarter 1996 up 2.4 percent compared to equivalent period in 1995.
- Manufacturing industrial orders rise three percent in October compared to the previous month.
- Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) consider plan to propose top rate of income tax between 45 and 47 percent. Current rate 53 percent.
HANDELSBLATT
- New growth figures are highest for more than a year.
- European Commisssion President Jacques Santer warns against delaying start of planned European economic and monetary union (EMU).
- Companies, banks and institutions form group to defend and improve Frankfurt's status as financial centre.
- SPD says Mauss affair has harmed reputation of German foreign policy.
SUEDDEUTSCHE ZEITUNG
- Red Army Faction says Christoph Seidler was never one of their guerrillas. Seidler is suspect in 1989 car-bomb killing of Deutsche Bank chief Alfred Herrenhausen.
- Cabinet approves German participation in new NATO-led Bosnian peace mission.
- Bavaria sends back group of Bosnian refugees, including for first time those not convicted of any crimes.
- German wholesalers say consumers will have to pay more for products from United States as deutschemark has weakened against the dollar.
DIE WELT

- Ethnic Germans driven out of Czechoslovakia at end of World War Two complain of lack of consultation in moves between Bonn and Prague to reach declaration on their fate and that of Czechs persecuted by the Nazis.
- SPD plans to increase its profile in 1997 to gear up for 1998 general elections.
- Exports driving force behind rise in third quarter economic growth.
